newsitem.title: CROATIA: Czech-style currency fall seen unlikely in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Czech-style currency fall seen unlikely in Croatia.

text.p: Croatia need not fear a speculative attack on its currency, the kuna, similar to that experienced recently by the Czech Republic, central bank officials and economists said on Thursday.

"We cannot say the kuna will never come under attack or how the central bank would react in such an event," Velimir Sonje, an executive director at the National Bank of Croatia, told Reuters at a conference on transition economies.
But, he said, speculators have no room to move against the kuna because of Croatia's low short-term debt. It stands at just around 500 million kuna (roughly $80 million).
"Even if the currency depreciated five or up to 10 percent, it would not be a catastrophe. Currency crises are not uncommon in some developed countries," he said.
What Sonje felt more nervous about, however, were inflation fears that might cause people to exchange their kuna funds for German marks to protect household savings.
The mark is still viewed as "the stable currency" in Croatia, and is the currency many people use for savings in banks and under the mattress.
"If all the people were suddenly to substitute kuna for marks, I would be worried," Sonje added.

For the moment Croatia is pursuing a relatively tight monetary policy to guard against inflation. Its exchange rate policy allows the kuna to fluctuate within an informal 2-3 percent band around a nominal peg of 3.7 kuna against the mark -- at which it was introduced in May 1994.
The central bank intervenes by buying hard currency from local banks, particularly during the summer tourist season, to prevent the kuna from appreciating too far.
Like the Czech Republic, Croatia has attracted strong capital inflows and investments since stabilising the economy in 1993-1994.

Also recovering from decades under communism and a war in former Yugoslavia, it is running a high current account deficit of around seven percent of its GDP, which some economists at the conference have said could be a cause for concern.
The Czech central bank was forced to float the crown in late May after massive speculative selling by investors alarmed by widening trade and current account deficits.

"Any country is sensible to worry about its current account deficit if it displays a sharper movement or more lengthy movement than the people in the market are used to," Peter Stek of the World Bank, chairing a session on Croatia, told Reuters.
"But I think Croatia has people...who are fully aware of what's happening," he said. Croatia's exchange rate policy was equipped to deal with a possible crisis should one arise.
"Small open economies with a low rate of inflation are well advised to follow a rate of pegging to some important currency," Stek added.
Sonje said the central bank had no specific pre-set targets for the kuna exchange rate or the volume of its currency interventions. He described the exchange rate policy as a "managed float".

"We go by the demand for money and expected revenue from tourism and build them into our projections. But they are also subject to last minute discretionary changes at each (foreign exchange) auction," he said.
Stek said this came "pretty close" to pegging and appeared to be a good way to proceed.
